REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo HOUSTON/LOS ANGELES, Oct 15 (Reuters) – When the oil supertanker Esteem Explorer sails from the United States to Japan in late November, loaded with about 2 million barrels of crude, the journey will cost $81 million. The same journey would have cost $9.1 million last year, on average. Refiners process oil into fuel to move food, retail goods and construction materials, and rising costs are stoking inflation in countries that depend on imports. Every $10-per-barrel increase in shipping costs adds about 23 cents per gallon to gasoline, said Kenneth Medlock, a fellow in energy and resource economics at the Houston-based Baker Institute for Public Policy. On that basis, the Esteem Explorer’s shipping cost works out to at least 80 cents more per gallon of gasoline than last year, according to Reuters calculations. “Everything gets more expensive because that’s how we move stuff around.” Freight rates account for more than 40% of the price of US oil, based on Wednesday’s price around $95 per barrel, compared with 7% on average in 2025, according to LSEG shipping and oil price data.

It had led to a “reduction in the connectivity of container traffic for long-distance services operated at EU ports, compared with neighbouring countries not subject to European environmental regulations, measured in terms of the teu-mile parameter”. However, the British Ports Association (BPA) today argued that 2025’s volume growth seen at the UK’s three main ports was caused by a combination of new capacity coming onstream at London Gateway and the reorganisation of the deepsea shipping alliances that took place at the start of the year.

items.title: Low Rhine water level driving barge cargo to capacity-strained road and rail
items.original_title: Low Rhine water level driving barge cargo to capacity-strained road and rail
items.summary: Terminals at Antwerp and Rotterdam are coming under growing pressure as unseasonably low water along the Rhine continues to restrict container barge movements on the river, with cargo being pushed towards already-constrained rail and road networks. SeasC4U’s Gunther Ginckels told The Loadstar barges around Duisburg-Ruhrort were operating at roughly two-thirds of normal capacity, while vessels further upstream were carrying substantially smaller loads. “Some services are suspended further upstream on the Kaub gauge, where low water has severely restricted navigation, while large volumes are being shifted to rail and truck, but alternative capacity is limited,” said Mr Ginckels. “Cargo is still moving, but carrying capacity is sharply reduced, transport costs have risen, transit times are longer and less predictable, while inland terminals, rail networks, and trucking markets are absorbing displaced cargo at higher cost and delays.” Some 35% of box movements along the Dutch hinterland tend to travel by inland waterway, meaning that even seeing a part of that traffic transferred to alternative modes piles massive pressure onto already constrained transport networks. Back in August, Metro Global stated that more than 200 trucks would be required to replace lost barge capacity, and while low water levels have become part and parcel of the Rhine’s summer months in recent years, the persisting into October presented additional problems.

Since mid-August US trucking and logistics firms have blamed tight drayage capacity as the biggest brake on growth and warned of bottlenecks at ports and inland rail ramps. The biggest factor has been the tightening trucking sector, exacerbated by a seasonal shift of drivers from drayage to the longhaul sector, in response to peak volumes. Paul Brashier, VP of global supply chain at ITS Logistics, an Echo company, reported that dray rates in Houston had shot up 40% over the past four months – albeit from a low base. items.title: LD Armateurs unveils world’s first six-sail cargo ship
items.original_title: LD Armateurs unveils world’s first six-sail cargo ship
items.summary: French shipowner LD Armateurs has completed the installation of six Norsepower rotor sails on Spirit of Toulouse, creating what it says is the world’s first cargo vessel fitted with six mechanical sails. The ship, being built in China for Airbus logistics work, is the lead vessel in a three-ship series designed to transport large aircraft sub-assemblies between Europe and North America. LD Armateurs said the six 35 m by 5 m rotor sails had now been installed at a coastal outfitting site in Shanghai by Wuchang Shipbuilding Industry Group, ahead of upcoming sea trials. The installation gives Spirit of Toulouse the highest number of mechanical sails yet fitted to a commercial cargo ship, and makes it the largest roro vessel equipped with wind propulsion, according to the company and rotor sail supplier Norsepower. The wind-assist system will work alongside two dual-fuel main engines and two dual-fuel generator sets capable of running on e-methanol, bio-methanol or marine diesel oil. LD Armateurs said the combination of methanol capability and wind propulsion was designed to cut fuel consumption and emissions on the vessel’s transatlantic route rather than rely on a single decarbonisation technology. “Spirit of Toulouse is much more than a new vessel,” said Samira Draoua, chief executive of LD Armateurs.

items.title: An Ageing Fleet Needs Greater Care
items.original_title: An Ageing Fleet Needs Greater Care
items.summary: Shipping is investing heavily in the next generation of vessels, fuels and propulsion technologies, but a large part of the existing fleet will still be trading well into the next decade. This will mean the steel structure must be protected for much longer. For instance, Clarksons data from July 2025 showed that 38% of global fleet capacity was more than 15 years old, including 30% of bulk carrier capacity and 33% of containership capacity. PATCH TESTS A three-year comparative trial aboard a 15,300TEU containership provides one example. Steelpaint’s single component zinc-rich polyurethane system was applied to a lashing bridge during drydocking in March 2023. At inspection in July 2026, the coated area showed only minor corrosion and required no crew maintenance. In the year up to June 2026, Stelpant has been trialled on some 16 bulk carriers with many going on to order full coats. An older ship is not necessarily a corroded ship, just as corrosion does not automatically make a vessel structurally unsafe. But with substantial proportions of the bulker and containership fleets already beyond 15 years, corrosion protection should increasingly be viewed as part of through-life asset management.

items.summary: Cyprus needs a coordinated strategy for shipping, energy and environmental protection to support port investment and modernisation, Cyprus shipping agents association president Reginos Tsanos said, warning that separate planning and regulatory priorities risk undermining commercially viable projects. Speaking at the Italy-Cyprus Maritime Business Forum, held at the DP World Limassol passenger terminal, Tsanos called for closer cooperation between government authorities, energy providers, municipalities and the maritime industry. According to a statement issued by the association on Wednesday, he said the three sectors were closely connected but often operated with different priorities, decision-making processes and timelines. Tsanos identified five areas for closer cooperation, including transforming ports into smart energy hubs, aligning regulatory frameworks, integrating investment planning across the blue economy, developing a shared maritime digital platform and coordinating marine spatial planning. However, he warned that “the capacity of Cyprus’ electricity networks remained a major challenge”, requiring coordinated planning between the state, local authorities, shipping companies and energy providers. At the same time, Tsanos argued that “assessing maritime, energy and environmental projects together could improve investment viability and risk management, rather than treating each development separately.” He also proposed a shared maritime digital platform to improve infrastructure planning, accelerate decisions and strengthen environmental monitoring.

items.title: Cyber-crime group hits 38 shipping and port groups with data leak threat
items.original_title: Cyber-crime group hits 38 shipping and port groups with data leak threat
items.summary: Cyber extortion group ‘n0n’ has named 38 organisations across the global shipping and ports sector on its dark-web leak site, raising concerns that data may have been stolen. Cybersecurity firm SOCRadar reported yesterday n0n published the listings in a single batch on 12 October, that included container terminals, shipping lines, port IT providers, and logistics businesses across 18 countries. The group emerged last month, listing 21 organisations across sectors including telecoms, retail, pharmaceuticals, and education. SOCRadar said the pattern of data described in the listings suggested a possible common point of entry, rather than 38 separate network intrusions. The amounts did not appear to correspond with the volume of data allegedly stolen: EUSU Logistics faced a $14m demand for 60mb, with ILCS Pelindo at $2.4m for 2.4gb. Of its 21 earlier victims, SOCRadar said 19 remained at the claimed stage, one was listed as negotiating, and one, Chibitek, had experienced a data leak. SOCRadar warned that maritime businesses that exchange EDI with companies named in the attack should plan for the possibility that their operational data could appear in the 19 October release. It advised them to identify the port community systems, EDI hubs, and file-transfer services handling their data; to check with providers for potential breaches, patch exposed systems, and investigate unusual access or bulk downloads.

items.title: Shipping firms and ports caught in mass cyber extortion claim
items.original_title: Shipping firms and ports caught in mass cyber extortion claim
items.summary: A cyber extortion group has threatened to publish data it claims it stole from 38 shipping, port, and logistics companies unless they pay multimillion-dollar ransoms by October 19. Cybersecurity firm SOCRadar said the group, known as n0n, added the 38 organisations to its dark web leak site in a single batch on October 12, marking a sharp shift towards maritime targets. The list includes 12 port and container terminal operators, 10 shipping lines and ship operators, port IT providers, logistics companies, and other maritime businesses across 18 countries. n0n is described as a financially motivated data-theft extortion operation rather than a conventional ransomware group. The group is threatening to release the alleged stolen material at 13:27 UTC on October 19. SOCRadar said ransom demands it reviewed ranged from $2.4m to $14m, payable in Bitcoin. In one example SOCRadar cited, Eurogate Tanger was allegedly asked to pay 10% of a $6m demand before being given access to a private negotiation room. The data n0n claims to possess varies between companies and includes EDI archives, container manifests, vessel schedules, gate movement records, commercial documents, internal system configurations, employee accounts, and financial records. SOCRadar said the relatively small, application-specific datasets claimed for several victims could indicate a common application or shared vulnerability rather than 38 separate compromises, although this too remains unconfirmed.

Crude oil production shut-ins averaged 4.8 million b/d in September, down from 5.8 million b/d in August, the EIA assessed. Container ships must carry containers on deck, making it difficult to install wind-assisted propulsion systems. items.title: SmartSea links crew travel and gangway access in dual launch
items.original_title: SmartSea links crew travel and gangway access in dual launch
items.summary: Maritime technology provider SmartSea has launched two connected platforms aimed at simplifying crew changes, linking journey planning with digital identity checks at ports and vessel gangways. SmartJourney brings together flight information, ground transport, accommodation, vessel schedules and crew rosters in one interface. It tracks travel status in real time, allowing crewing teams to respond to missed connections and schedule changes before they disrupt crew handovers. Companion product SmartAccess handles entry permissions at terminal gates, gangways and offshore installations. The platform checks personnel credentials, required certifications and authorisations against access requirements, including those associated with the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code. It can also be paired with SmartSea’s FacePod biometric units to match arriving seafarers and contractors with authorised personnel records, reducing reliance on manual documentation checks. “Crew movements involve ongoing coordination between travel coordinators, port agents, technical managers, and vessels,” said SmartSea CEO Kris Vedat. “When systems operate independently, small itinerary changes can create scheduling difficulties and extra administrative work.” SmartSea said the platforms provide operators with a connected view of who is expected to arrive, their current transit status and whether they have the necessary clearance to board. Both products are being offered to commercial shipping fleets, offshore support vessels, marine terminals and offshore energy facilities.

items.summary: Nasdaq-listed Greek shipowner Pyxis Tankers has agreed to acquire the remaining 40% stake in one of its ultramax bulkers from a company linked to its chairman and chief executive, Eddie Valentis. The deal, valued at approximately $6.83m before a separate working capital adjustment, will give Pyxis full ownership of the company holding the 2016-built Japanese ultramax Konkar Ormi . The 63,250 dwt, scrubber-fitted vessel was acquired for $28.5m in October 2023 through a joint venture in which Pyxis took a 60% controlling interest and a Valentis-affiliated company acquired the balance. The latest transaction values the bulker at approximately $32.08m, based on three independent shipbroker appraisals. After deducting $15m of vessel-related debt, the ship’s net appraised equity value stands at approximately $17.08m, putting the minority stake at $6.83m. Pyxis entered the dry bulk market in 2023 through the original joint venture with Valentis, subsequently expanding its exposure with two kamsarmax acquisitions. The company currently operates three bulk carriers alongside three MR product tankers.

items.title: The floating container platform turning heads
items.original_title: The floating container platform turning heads
items.summary: Every so often a ship comes along that makes even seasoned shipping watchers look twice. Meet the Fan Zhou 8, an extraordinary floating container platform that has just carried more than 3,000 teu out of China. According to Alphaliner, German independent carrier Carrier53′ Shipping chartered the 2024-built, 58,405 dwt heavy-load deckship from China’s Jiangsu Fanzhou Shipping for a September loading at Taicang, near Shanghai. The boxes were arranged in 17 bays and 20 rows, stacked five tiers high, with just two tiers on the outer rows. The voyage was arranged in cooperation with container trader Lotus Containers. Carrier53′ specialises in unconventional cargo movements, including oversized 53 ft containers manufactured in China for the North American market. The Fan Zhou 8 headed towards the Red Sea after loading, although its final destination has not been disclosed. Sea Legend’s 1,480 teu Tiger Maanshan recently reached Felixstowe and Rotterdam after sailing from China via the Northern Sea Route. Unlike the Fan Zhou 8, however, that vessel was specifically designed to carry LNG tank containers.

items.title: Tsakos returns to containership contracting in China
items.original_title: Tsakos returns to containership contracting in China
items.summary: Greek shipping group Tsakos has returned to the containership newbuilding market, emerging behind an order for two 3,200 teu vessels at China’s Hengli Heavy Industries. The pair appear in the Athens-based owner’s latest fleet register, with both scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2028. Both will be scrubber-fitted and equipped with alternative maritime power systems, allowing them to connect to shore-side electricity while alongside. The deal marks Tsakos’ first return to boxship contracting since 2022, when the group booked a series of approximately 2,800 teu vessels at HD Hyundai Mipo in South Korea. The ships are scheduled for delivery in 2028 and were reported at about $78m apiece. Tsakos’ fleet now stands at 112 vessels including newbuildings, with a 23-ship orderbook spanning tankers, LNG carriers, dry bulk vessels and the latest containership pair. The Greek owner is not alone in targeting Hengli’s 3,200 teu design. German non-operating owner Elbdeich Reederei has now also been linked by shipbuilding sources to two 3,200 teu ships at Hengli, again for 2028 delivery. The pair are reported at about $48m each, matching the market indications around the Tsakos vessels.

items.title: Hormuz shock briefly makes biofuel the cheapest bunker option
items.original_title: Hormuz shock briefly makes biofuel the cheapest bunker option
items.summary: The upheaval in global energy markets caused by the war in the Middle East has produced an unexpected winner in the marine fuels market, with biodiesel briefly emerging as the cheapest bunkering option in Rotterdam once European carbon costs are factored in. A new white paper from energy pricing specialist General Index and the London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) reveals that B30, a blend of 30% used cooking oil methyl ester (UCOME) and 70% very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO), became $74.61 per tonne cheaper than conventional VLSFO in April. The calculation incorporates EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) allowances and potential FuelEU Maritime penalties. In the preceding three months, B30 had been between $11 and $27 per tonne more expensive than conventional VLSFO on the same basis. The researchers also found that B100 UCOME, after incorporating carbon costs, traded at a discount to marine gasoil for eight weeks between March and May. The reversal came as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent fossil fuel prices soaring. SAF prices jumped $636 per tonne between February and March despite having supply chains largely independent of Hormuz. The findings highlight a widening difference between shipping and aviation.

items.title: Elisabeth Braw: The Undersea War
items.original_title: Elisabeth Braw: The Undersea War
items.summary: A ship’s anchor can wreak havoc on the world’s undersea infrastructure, something that has provided plenty of rich material for Splash reporting in recent years. For Elisabeth Braw, the Cook Islands-flagged tanker Eagle S provides one of the most brazen examples. On Christmas Day 2024, the vessel was accused of dragging its anchor 90 km across the Gulf of Finland seabed, severing the Estlink 2 power link and four telecommunications cables before Finnish authorities intervened. That collision between maritime law and an emerging security threat runs through Braw’s new book, The Undersea War: The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World , published by John Murray this month. Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads research into threats to the global maritime order, started writing in October 2024, having followed the subject for considerably longer. The 2022 Nord Stream pipeline explosions remain in the headlines. The Eagle S affair followed the Yi Peng 3 cable investigation and has been succeeded by further suspected anchor-dragging incidents in the Baltic. The book ranges from the Baltic to the Pacific, drawing on interviews with naval officers, undersea engineers and cable operators to show just how dependent modern economies have become on infrastructure that is difficult to monitor and harder still to defend.

items.title: Freight surge traps Americas heavy crude as Asia chases supply

items.summary: While Brent, the global benchmark for crude oil, is topping $100 a barrel, an unusual glut of heavy crude (high-density oil used to produce diesel, gasoline, and more) is building in North and South America. Competition to secure crude continues in Asia and Europe, but freight rates for tankers have surged in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war, making it harder to ship excess heavy crude from the Americas. In the Americas, crude supply has increased, but additional processing capacity at refineries is limited, causing inventories to pile up. But lately, even as heavy crude prices fall, refiners in Asia and Europe are finding it difficult to buy. Shipping to Asia costs $40 a barrel; even cheap crude is hard to export The biggest reason is the spike in tanker freight rates. Last week, the cost to ship crude from the Americas to Asia on a very large crude carrier topped $80 million (about 107.5 billion won). Scott Shelton, an energy specialist at energy broker TP ICAP, told Reuters, “The key is the shipping cost,” adding, “There is demand for tankers, but rates are rising and the number of available vessels is shrinking.” As shipping costs rise, prices for heavy crude from the Americas have fallen.

items.title: The Confidence To Act: Why R&D And Lifecycle Support Are The Real Enablers Of Fleet Decarbonisation
items.original_title: The Confidence To Act: Why R&D And Lifecycle Support Are The Real Enablers Of Fleet Decarbonisation
items.summary: Industry analysis suggests that roughly two-thirds of the existing global fleet will not undergo major retrofits for next-generation fuels, primarily because of vessel age and the economics involved. For this majority, the industry needs solutions that deliver measurable emissions reductions today, without introducing operational risk or requiring capital commitments that cannot be justified. One approach to this challenge is in adopting a layered strategy, one that matches the right solution to the right vessel, at the right point in its lifecycle. Fuel supply systems are an enabler of that strategy, and the confidence to invest in them depends, more than anything else, on the quality of the engineering, R&D and lifecycle support that underpins them. Documented, applied research into how alternative fuels behave in practice, and how fuel supply systems must be designed to handle them, is the foundation on which ship owner confidence is built. This is why lifecycle services are integral to the value of any decarbonisation investment, not an optional extra. In a sector defined by long asset cycles and the need to make durable capital decisions under uncertainty, that matters. R&D provides the foundation, and lifecycle support sustains it. Together, they give ship owners the confidence that their decarbonisation strategy remains resilient as the transition unfolds.

items.summary: The project will explore how hybrid-electric propulsion and GTT NEXT1®cargo containment system technology could support potential improvements in LNG transport efficiency. Lloyd’s Register (LR), Shell and GTT have launched a Joint Development Project (JDP) to develop a conceptual 200,000m³ LNG carrier combining hybrid-electric propulsion with GTT NEXT1® cargo containment technology. By bringing together a larger-capacity vessel concept with hybrid-electric propulsion and GTT NEXT1® cargo containment technology, the partners aim to explore how future LNG carrier designs could transport more cargo, operate more efficiently and provide greater flexibility as industry requirements continue to evolve. Under the JDP, the partners will work on the development and safety verification of the vessel’s hybrid-electric propulsion system, focusing on system architecture, redundancy philosophy and battery integration, while also exploring the commercial evaluation from a total cost of ownership (TCO) model. In parallel, the integration of GTT NEXT1® cargo containment technology will be assessed as part of the overall vessel concept. The project will also establish technical requirements and guidance for hybrid-electric propulsion in LNG carrier applications, helping to support further technical understanding of the technology.

The purchase is being funded entirely from internal cash and will have no effect on group gearing. The latest purchase takes LFG’s disclosed spending on ultramaxes to around $75.3m in little more than three months. Splash reported in July that the former Icon Offshore had made its first move into the segment with the $52.32m acquisition of two 2017-built ships, the Tian Mu Shan and Yan Dang Shan , from Chinese sellers. The pair came in at about $26.16m apiece. In June it agreed to pay $15.5m for the 2012-built, 56,735 dwt supramax Sea Affluence , taking disclosed spending on bulker acquisitions since June to about $90.8m. Managing director Lim Chern Wooi said the ultramax sector offered long-term opportunities as LFG develops into a more diversified maritime group. The company currently says it owns and operates 12 OSVs and 41 marine transportation assets spanning bulk carriers, tugs and barges.

items.summary: Chinese bulker owner Fujian Guohang Ocean Shipping is preparing to establish 12 wholly owned shipping companies in Hong Kong as it lays the groundwork for a newbuilding investment programme valued at approximately CNY2.49bn ($372m). The Beijing Stock Exchange-listed company disclosed on October 12 that its board had approved the creation of the subsidiaries through Guohang Ocean Shipping (Hong Kong) Holdings. Each company will have registered capital of $100,000, giving the proposed structure combined subscribed capital of $1.2m. Guohang has estimated the six-vessel investment at CNY2.49bn ($372m) and intends to raise up to CNY700m ($105m) through a private share placement. Of the proposed proceeds, CNY680m ($102m) has been earmarked for the vessels, with the remaining CNY20m ($3m) allocated to working capital. The Hong Kong restructuring comes just weeks after Guohang abandoned plans for a secondary listing on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. In September, the company said it would instead pursue a domestic equity placement to support fleet investment and strengthen its capital structure. Guohang has traditionally concentrated on dry bulk shipping, with its latest investment plans signalling an expansion into product tankers and specialised multipurpose tonnage. The new Hong Kong companies will also provide additional capacity for future shipowning arrangements beyond the initial six-vessel programme.

items.title: Bluecore takes nuclear barge plan beyond the drawing board
items.original_title: Bluecore takes nuclear barge plan beyond the drawing board
items.summary: US maritime nuclear startup Bluecore Energy has secured low-enriched uranium for its first floating power system as it moves ahead simultaneously with fuel, regulatory and class work. The Long Beach-based company has purchased uranium hexafluoride, or UF₆, enriched to 4.95% uranium-235 through nuclear fuel intermediary WMC. The material is being held at an undisclosed US nuclear fuel facility outside California while Bluecore works towards fuel fabrication, testing and validation. The move takes Bluecore another step beyond engineering and non-fuelled prototype work as it develops a compact water-cooled reactor designed from the outset for deployment on a floating platform. WMC buys, sells, stores, finances and transports materials across the nuclear fuel cycle, including enriched uranium products typically containing up to 5% uranium-235. Bluecore held its first pre-application meeting with the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission in August, presenting the reactor concept and discussing a potential licensing route. California planning records show the startup has leased warehouse, landside and submerged space at the port for its research operation and barge testing. The work sits within a wider US effort to bring nuclear technology into commercial maritime applications. Bluecore founder and chief executive Kofi Asante said the latest step is part of building the fuel, testing, engineering, safety, regulatory and class pathways together rather than sequentially.

items.title: IMOS Fuel Types Expand from Six to Ten to Support Growing Operational Complexity
items.original_title: IMOS Fuel Types Expand from Six to Ten to Support Growing Operational Complexity
items.summary: A changing fuel landscape The fuels powering vessels have shifted sharply in recent years, and the first shift was regulatory. Heavy fuel oil made up about 79% of international shipping fuel consumption in 20181 until the International Maritime Organization (IMO) cut the sulfur limit from 3.50% to 0.50% in 2020.2 Singapore, the world’s largest bunkering port and an indicator of the global market, shows how fast the market moved: low-sulfur fuel oil rose from under 1% of bunker sales in 2018 to 63% in 2020.3 Then the market shifted again. Scrubbers brought high-sulfur fuel back,3 and HSFO reached 29.5% of fuels tested by Veritas Petroleum Services (VPS) in 2023,4 alongside 54.3% VLSFO and 14.2% MGO. Biofuel blends, LNG, LPG, and methanol add further fuel types, and biofuel volumes tested by VPS rose 50% in 2025, to 1.2 million MT.5 Regulation, which triggered the previous shifts, is now driving the next one. Expanded fuel types in IMOS To keep pace with these shifts, IMOS now supports up to ten fuel types per vessel, up from six. The same limit applies to time charter contracts, so a long-term charter can reflect the vessel’s full fuel configuration.

items.title: 1 in 12 Ocean Shipments Has a Blank Carrier ETA
items.original_title: 1 in 12 Ocean Shipments Has a Blank Carrier ETA
items.summary: Tradlinx, a supply chain data platform based in South Korea, today released findings from an analysis of more than 500,000 ocean container shipments a year, showing that carrier ETAs are not only inaccurate but frequently missing. Carriers left the ETA blank in 42,832 cases, or 8.43% of shipments, most often while cargo was waiting at a transshipment port. Across more than 500,000 shipments a year, carriers left the ETA blank in 42,832 cases. The ETA for the intermediate transshipment port was missing in 30,929 cases (6.09%), the final-destination ETA of transshipment cargo in 6,168 cases (1.21%), and the destination ETA of direct shipments in 5,735 cases (1.13%). In this group of 25,341 shipments (4.99%), the average carrier ETA error was 90.0 hours. Our data points to a more basic gap: for roughly one in twelve shipments, the ETA simply goes missing somewhere along the way,” Tradlinx said. The model produced an estimate wherever the carrier ETA was missing, and its average error came in 31.4% lower than that of carrier ETAs, at 10.6 hours versus 15.4 hours. The difference was largest where carrier ETAs went furthest off course: on shipments missed by 48 hours or more, average error fell from 90.0 hours to 9.2 hours.

Perpetual Next expects to take a final investment decision on its DeltaNor bio-methanol plant by the end of 2027, a company spokesperson told ENGINE. Permits are among the factors the decision depends on, the spokesperson added. On Monday, Perpetual Next and renewable hydrogen producer Lhyfe announced a memorandum of understanding to study supplying up to around 12,000 mt/year of renewable hydrogen to the plant. The hydrogen would come from a 120 MW project Lhyfe is developing in the same Delfzijl industrial area. Adding hydrogen to the gas DeltaNor makes from biomass could let the plant turn more of its carbon into methanol and raise output. Last month, Perpetual Next hired engineering firm Bilfinger to help bring the project to an investment decision. In this episode of The Loadstar Podcast, host Charlotte Goldstone speaks to Erik Muttersbach, founder of Zauber and former Forto technology executive, about where AI and agentic AI really stand today, what is already happening in forwarding, and what could change over the next three to five years. Erik shares what he is learning from real-world deployments with customers, tackles some of the biggest misconceptions around AI, and explains why adoption and change management may be just as important as the technology itself. They also discuss the buy-versus-build question, the patterns Erik has seen across a decade of technology adoption in forwarding, and how companies can separate genuine AI capability from the hype. Looking ahead, what will AI actually change across the forwarding value chain – and which parts of the industry will prove hardest to transform? items.title: Iran threatens ships going dark in Hormuz
items.original_title: Iran threatens ships going dark in Hormuz
items.summary: Iran has warned that merchant ships switching off their identification and tracking equipment during what it deems unauthorised passages through the Strait of Hormuz will be treated as hostile, raising the stakes for vessels navigating one of the world’s most dangerous stretches of water. The warning comes as fresh details emerge of a wave of attacks on Sunday that extended beyond tankers to containerships. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) issued four retrospective alerts on Monday covering three tankers and a containership struck on October 11, bringing the day’s reported total to six. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), meanwhile, claimed to have attacked a VLCC attempting to transit without permission, releasing footage purportedly showing the fire-damaged, 298,800 dwt Al Maqam , owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services. It remains unclear whether the purported strike was among those reported by UKMTO or represents another incident. Two Indian seafarers remain missing after Sunday’s drone strike on the Nicaragua-flagged Petro Dolphin off Sohar, Oman. Nine crewmembers were rescued. The latest violence follows Saturday’s American airstrike against the Panama-flagged Ocean Molica in the Gulf of Oman, with Washington accusing the vessel of attempting to breach its naval blockade of Iranian ports.

items.summary: Petros Panagiotidis-controlled Robin Energy has taken a minority stake in Trafigura-backed Volare Shipping, adding indirect exposure to the VLCC market through the newly listed Oslo tanker owner. The Nasdaq-listed LPG carrier owner disclosed in a US Securities and Exchange Commission filing that it had participated in Volare’s private placement. Robin acquired 90,000 shares at NOK154 each, putting the investment at NOK13.86m ($1.45m). The investment follows Volare’s $500m capital raise and its move onto Euronext Growth Oslo earlier this month. Trafigura launched the shipping company in September to hold its expanding VLCC portfolio. Volare raised approximately $500m through an oversubscribed equity placement priced at NOK154 per share, valuing the company at around NOK11.5bn ($1.2bn) after the fundraising. The proceeds are intended to support outstanding newbuilding commitments, debt reduction and other corporate requirements. The company previously held a tanker alongside its gas carriers before selling that vessel earlier this year. In September, affiliated owner Toro outlined another fleet reshuffle involving the proposed separation of its remaining LPG vessels into a standalone Nasdaq-listed company.

items.title: French marines swoop on former Sovcomflot tanker in the Indian Ocean
items.original_title: French marines swoop on former Sovcomflot tanker in the Indian Ocean
items.summary: France has taken its crackdown on Russia’s shadow fleet into the Indian Ocean, boarding a former Sovcomflot aframax more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion. French marines descended by helicopter onto the 110,119 dwt DF Peak on Monday after authorities questioned the validity of its claimed Benin registration. President Emmanuel Macron said the vessel was suspected of sailing under a false flag and involvement in illicit fuel transportation. “France is determined to combat the shadow fleet, wherever it may be in the world,” Macron declared. The French military said the boarding was conducted under Article 110 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which permits inspections of vessels suspected of lacking valid nationality. Built in 2006, the tanker previously traded as NS Captain for Russian state-controlled Sovcomflot before becoming Kaliningrad in 2024 and subsequently DF Peak. The vessel has been under EU sanctions since June 2024 and is also blacklisted by Washington and London. Ukrainian intelligence links the ship to Russian crude exports. The operation follows several French interventions against Russia-linked tankers in European waters, including the interception of the Deliver off Sicily in June.

items.title: Washington teams up with ABS to accelerate nuclear shipping
items.original_title: Washington teams up with ABS to accelerate nuclear shipping
items.summary: The US Department of Energy (DOE) has joined forces with classification society ABS to accelerate the development of commercial nuclear-powered shipping and floating power plants. The agreement with DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy covers feasibility studies for floating reactors, dedicated nuclear shipping corridors and the ports, shipyards and industrial infrastructure required to build and support nuclear-powered vessels. ABS will co-manage the Maritime Nuclear Applications Group, providing technical, regulatory and economic expertise, while coordinating related work through the US Maritime Administration’s Center for Maritime Innovation. “Advanced nuclear technology is moving from concept to application, and the maritime industry needs to be ready for it,” said ABS chairman and CEO John McDonald. In 2022, DOE contracted ABS to examine barriers to commercial nuclear propulsion, while the class society subsequently published the industry’s first comprehensive rules for floating nuclear power plants. As Splash reported in July, ABS approved in principle a South Korean 15,000 teu containership concept incorporating a molten salt reactor, following earlier approvals for floating nuclear power modules developed by HD Hyundai. Last month, ABS backed a study examining the economics of a 174,000 cu m nuclear-powered LNG carrier. The vessel would cost approximately 2.5 times as much to build as a conventional LNG carrier, although researchers projected lower lifetime costs under certain carbon-pricing scenarios.

items.summary: Oslo-listed seismic specialist TGS, in joint venture with SLB, has announced the Pelotas Sul Phase 2 multi-client 3D survey offshore southern Brazil. The survey will cover about 11,200 sq km, and a Ramform Titan-class vessel is scheduled to begin data acquisition in October 2026, with completion in the second or third quarter of 2027. Building on Pelotas Sul Phase 1, acquired earlier this year, the new survey will further expand TGS’ high-quality 3D seismic coverage in a frontier basin that continues to attract industry interest. Geological analogues along the conjugate margin support the Pelotas Basin, and discoveries in Namibia de-risk it. The basin offers a broad range of underexplored play concepts, including turbidite systems, deep-water channels, and stratigraphic and structural traps. Pelotas Sul Phase 2 includes a balanced mix of held and open acreage. This provides data coverage relevant to companies evaluating existing acreage, while also creating opportunities linked to future licensing rounds and potential farm-in activity. “The project will provide additional high-quality subsurface insight across both held and open acreage, supporting our customers as they evaluate existing positions and future exploration opportunities in the southern Pelotas Basin,” said Kristian Johansen, CEO of TGS.
